text: From the same principle arises a further commendation, which Johnson gives with his accustomed plainness: "Shakespeare has no heroes; his scenes are occupied only by men" (Johnson 1765). He means that the persons of the drama are ordinary men, and that Shakespeare refused a practice which, in Johnson's judgement, prevailed with other dramatists; they raised their characters above the common level of humanity, furnished them with sentiments which no real person would express, and gave them a manner of speech contrived rather to exact admiration than to produce belief. This refusal Johnson counts among Shakespeare's chief merits. His characters speak as the reader himself would have spoken, had the same situation enclosed him and the same pressure borne upon him; their words are drawn from ordinary life, and they affect us because we recognise in them our own nature. Nor is this truth lost when the incident is improbable or supernatural. Ghosts and witches are beyond ordinary experience; but the speech of those who behold them remains within it. The marvel is in the plot, while the dialogue keeps the level of life; Hamlet questions his father's ghost as any son might question so dreadful a thing, and Macbeth broods on the prophecy as an ambitious man would brood on the promise of a crown.
